data.title: Robots.txt
data.tagline: A root-level file that tells automated crawlers which paths they may crawl
data.learningOutcome: You can tell whether a robots.txt rule affects crawling or user access, and know that sensitive pages need authentication and authorization.
data.description: Shopping carts and duplicate filter URLs can waste crawler requests, so robots.txt can describe crawling rules at the site root. It is guidance for crawlers that follow the rules, not a block on normal visitors, authentication, or protection for sensitive data.

learning.assumes: You know that search crawlers visit public sites and have seen paths that should not be crawled frequently.
learning.outcome: You can tell whether a robots.txt rule affects crawling or user access, and know that sensitive pages need authentication and authorization.

explanation.title: The file location sets its scope
explanation.text: robots.txt normally lives at the site root, such as https://example.com/robots.txt. Rules apply to the matching protocol, host, and port.

explanation.title: A crawler reads the rules before requesting
explanation.text: A compliant crawler uses User-agent, Allow, and Disallow to decide whether to request a path. A normal browser does not lose access because of this file.

data.boundary: Robots.txt is a crawling instruction, not permission control, and it is not the same as noindex in search results. Protect admin pages, orders, and customer data with authentication, authorization, and server-side checks rather than links hidden from navigation or Disallow alone.

lessonPractice.title: An admin page contains customer data, and the team wants to protect it with Disallow in robots.txt. What is the right judgment?

options.label: Protect the admin page with authentication and authorization, then use robots.txt only to reduce crawling if useful
options.feedback: Correct. Permissions decide who can access data; robots.txt is a crawling suggestion for compliant crawlers and cannot block people who know the URL.

options.label: Disallow is enough because a path hidden from crawlers cannot be accessed by anyone
options.feedback: Disallow is not a lock. People and non-compliant programs can still request the URL, so sensitive data cannot rely on it.

options.label: Remove the admin page from navigation instead of adding access control
options.feedback: Hiding a link only reduces discovery. It does not check identity or prevent direct access to a known URL.

data.agentPrompt: Create robots.txt at the site root to limit crawling of duplicate filter paths while keeping normal product pages crawlable. Check the file location, rule matches, and that a normal browser can still access the path. Protect admin pages and customer data with authentication and authorization, not Disallow.

references.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification
